title: LOB-Impact Benchmark: Emergent Market Impact in Generative Limit Order Book Models
abstract: Realistic market impact is essential for generative limit order book (LOB) models to serve as world models for trading agents. If a simulator misprices this mechanism, agents learn policies that are optimal in the simulator but wrong in the real market. Existing metrics assess generated streams purely through distributional comparison with historical data, leaving counterfactual response to an agent's own orders largely unexplored. Here, we show that market impact emerges naturally in neural LOB generators trained solely for next-token prediction. We inject execution-style metaorders into the generated message flow of five autoregressive models across five NASDAQ stocks and measure the response using estimators from the empirical impact literature, validated on baselines whose physics is known in advance. Our benchmark evaluates any message-level generator in three phases: free generation (reading order-flow persistence against price diffusivity); metaorder injection (yielding the impact law's exponent and amplitude); and a post-execution window (measuring relaxation). In addition, comparing each visible injection to a blind, simulator-only control isolates the model's learned response from standard book mechanics. For every model on every stock, we measure how the impact responds as a function of cumulative metaorder participation. Interestingly, we observe emergent impact in generative models of market data, with exponents in the range of 0.63 to 1.21, slightly above the traditional 0.5 of the square-root law of impact. In the family of models tested, we are so far unable to observe impact decay during relaxation. We tentatively attribute this to the still-short context windows of the models. We release the benchmark as open source to validate future generative models for market data.
why: Market impact benchmark for generative LOB models; grounded in NASDAQ order flow.

title: Testing semi-strong market efficiency in Brazilian football: A risk-adjusted machine learning approach
abstract: Using Brazilian Série A matches from 2012 to 2025, we compare seven machine learning forecasters, calibrated and validated walk-forward, against a low-margin bookmaker's closing price in the home-win market. Every architecture loses to the closing line on log loss, and an encompassing regression fails to reject efficiency in thirteen of fourteen cases. Three staking rules are then tested out of sample. A static half-Kelly rule compounds a signal with no edge into a loss of about ninety-four percent of capital, robust to the probability series, the model set and the friction assumption. A drawdown-constrained rule preserves capital only by staking almost nothing, and relaxing its risk limits raises leverage without producing a return distinguishable from zero. Calibration gains need not become information beyond the price, and compounding destroys capital fastest at zero edge. We detect no departure from efficiency at the resolution this design affords.
why: Walk-forward OOS test vs closing line; staking drawdown and friction discipline.

title: Inflation Narratives and Expectation Formation: Evidence from Large Language Model Embeddings
abstract: We develop a novel directional inflation narratives (DIN) index using large language model embeddings applied to Wall Street Journal articles from 1984 to 2024. The index captures whether inflation-related news points toward rising or declining inflation. We find that increases in DIN are followed by higher household inflation expectations and contain information about subsequent realized inflation. Using CPI announcement surprises as an instrument for daily DIN, we provide causal evidence that more inflationary narratives raise household inflation expectations. The relationship between DIN and inflation expectations is stronger when attention to inflation is high and among households with greater news exposure. Moreover, DIN helps explain forecast errors in inflation expectations and sheds light on time-varying information rigidities. Energy and labor feature prominently in inflation narratives, while the importance of other factors varies across episodes. The results are robust to concerns about LLM look-ahead bias, and the embedding-based measure consistently outperforms traditional text analysis methods. These findings show that the direction conveyed by news narratives shapes household inflation expectations and highlight the potential of LLM embeddings for extracting economically meaningful information from large-scale text.
why: LLM embedding inflation index with causal IV; macro, not trading-ready.

title: Ask Before You Judge: Output Format Determines Whether Small Open Models Detect Non-Compliant Green Bond Frameworks
abstract: Green bond frameworks are plausible targets for automated screening with large language models, and small open-weight models are the configuration that cost and confidentiality push institutions towards. We test whether such models can detect non-compliance with the ICMA Green Bond Principles, and whether the answer depends on how the question is asked. From ten public green bond frameworks we built 43 controlled cases: ten compliant summaries and 33 in which a single core component is defective. Four models scored every case at temperature zero under three output formats: (A) verdict first, then rationale; (B) component-by-component notes, then a verdict; (C) an explicit pass or fail judgement on each component, with the overall verdict derived by rule rather than generated. Format determined the result. Under A, the three open models approved 31, 33 and 33 of 33 defective frameworks, including every case that added new coal-fired power generation to eligible uses. Under C the same models, on the same cases, approved 9, 11 and 10. Format B was unreliable: it left Mistral 7B unchanged at 33 of 33 and broke Llama 3.1 8B's output structure on 17 of 43 cases. GPT-5.4 nano approved 2 of 33 under all three formats. The recovery was uneven. Missing reporting and a missing selection process were detected in 10 of 10 cases by every open model under format C, but no model detected the ineligible-use defect in more than 3 of 10 parsed cases. Format choice should be tested before any such system is deployed.
why: Tests small open LLMs on green bond screening; format effect is practical.

title: CARLAR Influence: A Structured Hallucination Risk in Multimodal Cheque Extraction and an Exploratory Compressed-Image Countermeasure
abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for structured extraction from financial documents, but their behavior under visual ambiguity is poorly understood. We study CARLAR (Courtesy Amount Recognition and Legal Amount Recognition) influence: a model returns the same amount for both cheque fields even though their annotations differ, including cases with a blank annotation encoded as zero. Across ten visual prompting conditions, we evaluate GPT-4.1 and Claude 4.5 Sonnet on 243 primary cheques (124 with two observed unequal amounts) and 598 strict mismatches from two additional datasets. Under courtesy redaction, GPT-4.1 CARLAR reaches 73.7 percent (95 percent bootstrap interval: 68.3 to 79.0; p below 0.001 versus baseline). Model-reported confidence can remain high when predictions agree; expected calibration error reaches 0.93 among CARLAR cases. We also test a compressed-image few-shot intervention that presents examples as one visual table without model fine-tuning. On the 243-case cohort, Claude's Control condition increases paired joint extraction accuracy by 11.5 percentage points (95 percent interval: 6.2 to 16.9; adjusted p = 0.00054), but its strict-124 gain is smaller and not significant after correction. The intervention's effect on predicted-field agreement is model-dependent: it decreases for Claude and increases for GPT-4.1. These results motivate validation methods that account for visual context and dependencies between extracted fields.
why: Multimodal LLM cheque hallucination with calibration failure; concrete finance eval.

title: The More the Better? A Comparison of Single- and Multi-Agent LLM Setups on a Financial Review Task
abstract: Practitioner guidance holds that a large language model reviews a document better when the work is divided among agents. We test a narrow form of it in a controlled comparison of single-agent and multi-agent setups on a financial task, reviewing credit assessment memos against requirements. One agent checks six requirements in one call. A team of three on the same model checks the same memo, two requirements each, in the same words, with no roles or later stage. Labels are known for every requirement on 300 synthetic memos, so misses and false alarms are measured separately. Two primary predictions are tested on four models at a Bonferroni-corrected level. Under an instruction to decide each requirement once, the team catches 0.08 to 0.10 more of the defects that carry an explanation on the three models whose single agent misses some, at the corrected level on two. It raises more false alarms on all four, at the corrected level on three. Balanced accuracy, an exploratory measure, changes by 0.02 or less, and the team uses 2.2 to 2.4 times the tokens. Showing each agent the requirements it was not given reduces the added false alarms on the two Claude models, at the corrected level on one. In exploratory comparisons, sampling the single agent three times and flagging on any draw gives higher balanced accuracy than the team on those models, and the team's results depend on the instruction.
why: Single vs multi-agent LLM credit memo review; tests a practitioner belief.

title: Expert-Guided Rubrics as Dense Reward Signals for Reinforcement Learning in Non-Verifiable Domains
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in non-verifiable domains such as financial services, where they must interpret user intent, rewrite queries, and retrieve information under domain-specific constraints. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can train such agents from the consequences of their actions, recent successes largely rely on verifiable tasks with automatically computed binary rewards. In non-verifiable retrieval tasks, assessing query quality requires scarce subject-matter expert (SME) judgment that is inherently graded rather than binary. With Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), sparse rewards yield no useful learning signal when all sampled outputs within a group receive the same outcome, causing optimization to stall. We introduce a method that converts a small, fixed investment of SME judgment into a dense reward and combines it with retrieval-based metrics to form a hybrid, GRPO-compatible training signal. Experiments show improvements of up to 6\% in Recall@3 and 6.7\% in MRR@3 compared with sparse-reward baselines.
why: Expert-rubric dense rewards for financial retrieval agents; limited evidence visible.

title: Cross-Lingual Reusability of LLM Pipelines: Financial Extraction, Multilingual Reasoning, and Semantic Screening
abstract: Financial institutions increasingly deploy large language models (LLMs) in multilingual markets, raising a practical question: can pipelines developed and validated in English be reused across languages, or must they be rebuilt per locale? We test cross-lingual reusability along three dimensions--accuracy, reasoning-effort transfer, and behavioural stability--through three complementary tasks. Task 1 (cheque extraction) and Task 2 (Mintaka QA with pinned evidence across nine languages and nine model-effort configurations) test whether accuracy and effort settings transfer; Task 3 (FinanceBench pilot, 50 items over SEC 10-K filings in four languages) validates whether these patterns generalise to financial content. Accuracy reusability is broadly confirmed: Gemini 3.5 Flash achieves 95.2-97.6% extraction accuracy across prompt languages, and FinanceBench per-language means span 5.8pp (77.1-82.9%), though the language-difficulty ranking reverses between domains (Hindi is worst on Mintaka, best on FinanceBench at 82.9%). Effort reusability is domain-dependent: higher reasoning effort yields marginal gains on general-knowledge QA but up to 8pp on financial content, and effort configurations that help in English help proportionally in other languages. Behavioural reusability holds: citation-set overlap with English averages 77-79% Jaccard, with no single language consistently worse. Together, these results support qualified reuse of English-built pipelines, but per-domain, per-language validation remains necessary--neither semantic similarity nor self-reported confidence reliably predicts cross-lingual accuracy.
why: Cross-lingual reuse of financial LLM pipelines; useful but incremental.

title: RGH-GNN : Risk-Gated Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network for Financial Fraud Detection
abstract: Credit card fraud is a significant problem for financial institutions, resulting in substantial monetary loss each year. Fraud patterns and methods are continuously evolving, with fraudulent transactions often disguised to resemble legitimate activity. Real world transaction data for fraud detection is severely affected by class imbalance making it harder to detect these transactions. Fraudulent transactions are rarely isolated. Accounts, devices, and other common attributes are often shared across fraudulent activity, revealing relational patterns that individual transaction features alone cannot capture. Graph-based approaches model these relationships explicitly. However, standard graph neural networks aggregate neighbourhood information uniformly, which can dilute the already scarce signal carried by fraudulent transactions and limit detection of camouflaged fraud. This work presents RGH-GNN, a heterogeneous graph neural network that addresses this limitation by incorporating transaction-level risk scores, generated by a supervised LightGBM classifier as edge weights. It is used to guide message passing through a learnable risk-gated aggregation mechanism. It ensures that high-risk transactions contribute more strongly to learned representations rather than being diluted by uniform neighbourhood aggregation. RGH-GNN is evaluated on the IEEE-CIS fraud detection dataset against standard graph neural network models that are trained on the same heterogeneous graph. RGH-GNN outperforms all baselines across every evaluation metric, with an AUC-ROC score of 0.914. This demonstrates that incorporating engineered risk signals into graph-based message passing substantially improves fraud detection performance.
why: Heterogeneous GNN for card fraud; graph signal but fraud not trading.

title: Deep catastrophic-risk-aware reinforcement learning
abstract: Estimating extreme risk in reinforcement learning becomes increasingly difficult as the confidence level increases, since only a small number of observations contribute to empirical estimates of Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). In this paper, we extend an Extreme Value Theory (EVT) approach for CVaR optimization to high-dimensional neural-network policies. Using a peaks-over-threshold representation and method-of-moments estimation, we obtain a differentiable tail-risk objective and show that, conditional on the selected threshold, its finite-sample gradient can be computed directly through automatic differentiation. We first validate the approach in a controlled experiment with a known optimal solution and then investigate its performance in a deep-hedging problem with rare extreme market movements. Our results show similar hedging behavior for EVT- and empirical-CVaR-trained policies under normal conditions, while EVT-trained policies exhibit lower hedging losses under the extreme-scenario evaluation across the training sample sizes considered. These results suggest that EVT can provide a practical alternative for training neural policies when the observations relevant to extreme risk are scarce.
why: EVT-based CVaR for deep hedging; competent but niche contribution.

title: Market Regime-Based Multi-Asset Portfolio Optimization Using Nested Clustered Optimization for Tactical Asset Allocation
abstract: We propose a regime-aware tactical asset allocation (TAA) framework integrating market regime detection with Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) for multi-asset portfolio construction. The central hypothesis is that incorporating market regime information into the NCO pipeline, specifically at the stages of covariance estimation, hierarchical clustering, and weight optimization, yields portfolios with improved risk-adjusted performance and reduced downside risk relative to regime-agnostic baselines. Market regimes (Bullish, Sideways/Neutral, Bearish) are detected using a Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (HMM) fitted exclusively on information available up to each decision point, thereby preventing look-ahead bias. Regime-conditional covariance matrices and clustering structures parameterize NCO at each rebalancing event. An adaptive rebalancing rule, triggered by regime transitions or material changes in optimal weights, replaces fixed-calendar rebalancing. The framework is evaluated on a heterogeneous monthly multi-asset universe comprising Indonesian government bonds (SBN), the LQ45 equity index, gold (IDR-denominated), foreign exchange (CNY/IDR), and Bitcoin/IDR (BTC). Out-of-sample performance is assessed via rolling walk-forward backtesting. Benchmarks include equal-weight (1/N), buy-and-hold, standard NCO without regime awareness, minimum variance, hierarchical risk parity (HRP), and a rule-based regime strategy. Performance metrics include cumulative return, annualized Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, maximum drawdown, Calmar ratio, turnover, and net-of-cost returns. Statistical significance is assessed using the Jobson-Korkie test. The empirical analysis indicates that the proposed regime-aware TAA framework successfully limits tail risk, achieving a maximum drawdown of 4.44% and demonstrating the utility of HMM-based regime detection in multi-asset risk management.
why: Regime HMM with NCO allocation; look-ahead guarded but forgettable.

title: Arithmetic Models for Commodity Futures, Vanilla, and Calendar Spread Options
abstract: We develop an arithmetic multi-factor stochastic volatility model for commodity futures and options. The arithmetic specification yields a low-dimensional Markovian representation of the futures curve and semi-closed-form pricing formulas for vanilla and basket options, including calendar spread options. These properties make the model suitable for large-scale empirical estimation. We estimate the model using an unscented Kalman filter on a panel of WTI crude oil futures, vanilla options, and calendar spread options spanning 2013-2024. We find that three stochastic volatility factors are needed to capture both the level and slope of the volatility term structure, and that hedges based on these factors remove almost all of the daily risk of a portfolio of vanilla options. Calendar spread options provide information about the dependence structure of futures prices that is not captured by futures and vanilla options alone. A model estimated without calendar spread options systematically overprices them by overstating the decorrelation between adjacent futures contracts. Including these options in the estimation brings the model's decorrelation close to the observed decorrelation, which removes the overpricing and improves their hedges, at only a small loss of accuracy in the pricing and hedging of vanilla options. Finally, we show that the arithmetic model fits futures and vanilla options better than its geometric counterpart and hedges the vanilla options slightly better.
why: Commodity futures/options model on WTI panel; solid but conventional.

title: Speculative Imbalance Positions by Non-Physical Traders: Impacts on Electricity System Balancing in Great Britain
abstract: The electricity system in Great Britain (GB) allows participants to deliberately produce or consume a different volume to their traded position and has incentivised this practice with a single imbalance price since 2015. In particular, non-physical traders (NPTs) often take an open position to imbalance without any intention to produce or consume power. However, new government proposals could restrict this practice due to concerns over supply-demand balancing feasibility and costs. This article presents the first empirical analysis of speculative imbalance positioning (SIP) by NPTs in the GB electricity system through its effects on imbalance volumes, balancing costs, the imbalance price, and associated settlement costs over the period 2021-2024. Our research uses party-level imbalance data in each settlement period to run counterfactual simulations of the electricity balancing mechanism without the aggregate NPT imbalance. Our results indicate that SIP by NPTs reduced the total net balancing volume required by 3.1-3.9 TWh (16-20%), reduced system imbalance standard deviation by 48-65 MWh (13-17%), reduced balancing costs by £347-396m (5.9-6.7%), and reduced supplier imbalance costs by £193-325m (65-75%) over the analysis period. These results suggest that consumer bills would have been higher without SIP by NPTs, since the extra costs would likely have been passed on to consumers through levies, although the potential for effects in the wholesale (primarily late-stage intraday) markets complicates this picture.
why: GB imbalance speculation counterfactuals on real settlement data; niche market.

title: How Attained-Age Recalibration Alters Retirement Portfolio Outcomes: Evaluating Drawdown Policies and Standard of Individual Living Through a Rolling Attained-Age Model
abstract: Most retirement research relies on a fatal flaw: assuming a single, unchanging 30-year plan. But retirees live in a dynamic world where age, wealth, and life expectancy shift annually. This paper, serves as a “proof of concept,” introduces a "rolling model" that recalibrates planning horizons and portfolios every year. By testing a couple retiring with $1.2 million against various strategies, the study exposes the hidden costs of common financial advice, as well as discussion points for client reviews. The results challenge conventional wisdom. Shifting to lower-volatility investments slightly reduced spending shortfalls, but slashed terminal wealth by over $500,000; though this was compared to the typical single period, single allocation model. Surprisingly, holding a one-year cash reserve to avoid selling stocks during market crashes actually increased the risk of lifestyle-threatening income gaps. There is no universal winner—only tradeoffs —based on client risk tolerance and capacity, as well as overall goals . All of which is specific to each unique client situation and desires. How does a reality-based, year-by-year recalibration, that models aging, transform everything we know about funding retirement? Using Academia’s Co-scientist AI led to programming approaches outside the traditional roadmaps of commercial software providers, by generating functional code structures distinct from conventional commercial development use cases.
why: Retirement drawdown simulation; practical but single-couple proof of concept.

title: S$^2$-MAS: A Society-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation Framework with 500 Million Household Persona Agents
abstract: Simulating economic responses at society scale requires agents whose decisions reflect household circumstances and the effects of earlier actions. We introduce S$^2$-MAS, a society-scale multi-agent simulation framework built on 500 million synthetic household personas grounded in real-survey data. Its Genese engine separates decisions from state updates, while reusable financial scenarios and application ledgers track consumption, cash, debt and payments. FinL-mlx, a compact decision model trained with SFT + RLCD on 2.93 million examples, achieves 74.55% accuracy and 38.37% question-macro F1 in consumer financial-choice scenarios, outperforming Jev 1.13 and GLM-5.3-Flash on both measures. We evaluate eight financial task families and simulate 12 million distinct household agents in paired purchase-funding conditions. Jointly raising purchase goals and approved credit limits increases consumption, with responses differing across age and income groups. Education, employment and household-size differences persist after age--income standardization and mainly reflect transitions from deferral to purchase. Asset and debt groups differ in cash drawdown, repayment and closing debt. A 24-month panel varies purchase goals under a common credit product, with repayment and arrears updating subsequent offers. S$^2$-MAS links heterogeneous household decisions to evolving consumption, cash and repayment paths, supporting economic experiments across household groups, population scales and time horizons.
why: Society-scale household agent simulation; large but weak validation visible.

title: Staged Continual Adaptation of Multimodal Foundation Models for Japanese Financial Documents
abstract: Staged post-training of multimodal foundation models chains vision-language alignment, reasoning distillation, and domain tuning, yet how each phase trades capabilities against the others remains under-characterised. Tracking an 8.4B-parameter model from an un-fine-tuned baseline through three training phases on Japanese financial documents (evaluated on five text-input benchmarks), we find the phases interact non-additively: math-only distillation overwrites the financial knowledge acquired earlier even as procedural math skill survives, and the domain phase repairs more than it installs. A skip-phase ablation is best for domain knowledge but forfeits numerical-reasoning gains, so per-phase contributions are not decomposable and the best checkpoint is task-dependent, with implications for checkpoint retention and scheduling rather than added stages.
why: Staged multimodal tuning on Japanese finance docs; interaction findings modest.

title: Cloud-Native MLOps Deep Learning Pipelines for Financial Risk Prediction in Transportation Infrastructure Capital Allocation
abstract: Financial risk prediction in transportation infrastructure capital allocation requires models that adapt to nonstationary macroeconomic conditions while meeting low-latency operational constraints. Traditional capital investment analyses often rely on static projections that do not account for structural shifts over multi-decade planning horizons. This paper describes an end-to-end cloud-native machine learning pipeline for infrastructure financial risk forecasting in transit-oriented development (TOD) corridors. By coupling a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network with a multi-head self-attention layer on AWS SageMaker, the system achieves a 93.7% risk classification accuracy with a 37-42 ms P95 inference latency and reduces monthly infrastructure costs by 67% compared to a provisioned on-premise baseline. The pipeline integrates a centralized feature store to synchronize offline and online feature transformations and uses automated drift monitoring based on the Population Stability Index to trigger retraining when economic indicators diverge from training baselines. On a 20-year longitudinal dataset covering 42 California TOD corridors (2005-2024), ablation experiments demonstrate that self-attention preserves predictive capability during macroeconomic shocks, particularly abrupt interest rate shifts. We also evaluate cloud ingestion controls, data governance requirements, and deployment architectures for continuous risk scoring.
why: Cloud MLOps pipeline with unverified accuracy; no finance baseline shown.

title: No Authorization, No Execution: The Production of Authorization Facts and the Starting-Point Gap in Accountability Infrastructure for Financial Agents
abstract: The guess-and-execute architecture of financial agents has a direct regulatory impact: it removes the object that supervisory checks, dispute resolution and resolution proceedings are designed to verify. That object is the authorization fact on which the EU financial regulatory complex depends, including GDPR, DORA, MiFID II, PSD2/PSD3 and the AI Act. Supervisory tools continue to operate, but the fact they are meant to verify is not produced at the point of execution. This is not a future risk. The EBA survey of September 2025 reports that 55 percent of surveyed banks already use general-purpose or agentic AI in consumer-facing processes. The first DORA annual report records 3,383 major ICT incidents in 2025 but does not separate failures caused by autonomous AI agents as an independent category. That absence is itself a visible form of the accountability gap in supervisory data. Because every rule presupposes prior authorization, supervisors face a choice among retroactive invalidation, ex post ratification, explicit exception and non-determination. The fourth path is operationally easiest and normatively least sustainable. It produces silent exceptionalization: rules remain in force, but their object contracts in proportion to the growth of agentic execution. The early applicability of Article 50 and the delayed application of Articles 12 to 15 add an internal time gap. That gap creates a compliance precedent in which formal disclosure can be satisfied while authorization facts remain absent. The legal cause is structural. A model's probabilistic interpretation is not a user's expression. Linguistic ambiguity makes ex post reconstruction of situated meaning impossible. Consent is not deficient in degree; it is absent at the point of production. The paper proposes intent determination as a production condition for authorization facts. The mechanism fixes the system's understanding before execution; treats auditability and reproducibility, rather than model confidence, as the test of whether consent is established; triggers principal confirmation only where audit cannot determine intent; locks confirmed intent as an immutable baseline; and suspends execution on deviation. Intent determination is necessary but not sufficient. It does not replace identity verification, AML, suitability assessment or other downstream compliance requirements. It gives those requirements an object that can be verified in the dimension of consent. The argument applies to all high-risk AI execution scenarios. Finance is the field where the consequences are least reversible and supervisory pressure most direct.
why: Regulatory position argument on financial agent accountability; no empirics.

title: Energy-Aware Benchmarking of Quantum Machine Learning for Financial Prediction Tasks: An Accuracy–Sustainability Pareto Analysis of Hybrid Quantum–Classical Pipelines
abstract: Quantum machine learning (QML) is increasingly proposed for financial forecasting and risk analysis, yet comparisons with classical methods almost always stop at accuracy and wall-clock time. As quantum systems approach deployment, their resource footprint — cryogenic cooling, repeated circuit executions, calibration and the classical optimiser loops surrounding them — becomes a first-order concern. This paper introduces an energy-aware benchmarking framework for hybrid quantum–classical ML pipelines and applies it to three financial tasks: credit-risk scoring (UCI German Credit) and next-day direction prediction for the S&P 500 and NIFTY 50 indices. Variational quantum classifiers (VQC) and quantum-kernel support vector machines (QSVM) at 4–8 qubits are compared with class-weighted logistic regression, RBF-SVM, random forest, XGBoost and a GPU-trained LSTM on identical data subsets. Classical energy is measured directly by a 10 Hz power sampler; quantum energy combines the measured optimisation-loop energy with a per-shot hardware cost model spanning optimistic to pessimistic scenarios. On credit risk the best quantum model (QSVM, 8 qubits) trails logistic regression by 7.8 balanced-accuracy points while consuming 7 × 1010 times its energy. On index direction all models, classical and quantum, perform at chance, so the 109× quantum energy premium purchases nothing. The gap is insensitive to the hardware assumption: break-even would require roughly 10-10 J per shot, ten orders of magnitude below current superconducting systems. Once the statistical uncertainty of the accuracy estimates is taken into account, no quantum model.
why: Quantum ML energy benchmark on standard tasks; limited finance utility.

title: Dynamic portfolio selection under range value-at-risk with logarithmic returns
abstract: This paper studies continuous-time portfolio selection under Range Value-at-Risk (RVaR), with both portfolio performance and risk evaluated in terms of logarithmic returns. We formulate a mean--RVaR problem in a continuous-time financial market and reduce the dynamic optimization to a static quantile problem. Using quantile representation, Lagrangian optimization, and convexification, we characterize the optimal terminal wealth through the convex envelope of an RVaR-specific transformed weighting function. The RVaR-specific convex envelope exhibits two distinct geometric configurations. Under Scenario~1, the terminal wealth has a VaR-type structure: the minimum-RVaR payoff is digital-option-like, whereas for $0<λ<1$ it consists of two growth-optimal regions separated by a constant-payoff region. Under Scenario~2, the convex envelope is determined either by a supporting line connecting an interior contact point to the endpoint or by a common supporting line with two interior contact points, leading to a richer multi-region payoff structure. We further show that the RVaR solutions reduce to their VaR and Expected Shortfall (ES) counterparts as $β\downarrowα$ and $α=0$, respectively. Under constant investment opportunities, we also derive closed-form wealth processes and replicating portfolio strategies. Numerical results show that the effects of $(α,β,λ)$ on risky-asset exposure are nonlinear and generally non-monotone. In particular, when $α>0$, pure minimum-RVaR optimization may assign zero terminal wealth in sufficiently bad states because the extreme quantile region $[0,α)$ is excluded from the RVaR criterion. These results clarify how interval-based quantile risk control shapes state-dependent portfolio payoffs and connects RVaR with its VaR and ES limiting cases.
why: Continuous-time RVaR portfolio theory; no data or implementation path.

title: Securing Agentic Commerce Through Behavior-Aware Fraud Detection and Cybersecurity for Trusted AI-Agent Payment Authorization
abstract: The growing use of autonomous artificial intelligence agents in digital commerce creates new security concerns involving agent impersonation, unauthorized payments, compromised agents, and misuse of delegated authority. This research introduces the Autonomous Commerce Agent Guard System (ACAGS), a cybersecurity framework combining supervised machine learning, behavioral analytics, agent-specific authorization controls, and explainable AI. The framework was evaluated using synthetic financial transaction data augmented with simulated agent characteristics and five adversarial scenarios. XGBoost was selected following comparisons with alternative classifiers. Across ten experimental runs, behavioral features improved mean F1-score from 52.12% to 67.49%, with agent-specific features increasing performance to 69.46%. The framework achieved detection rates of 99.77% for abnormal agent behavior, 99.73% for impersonation, and 100% for malicious delegation and authorization-scope violations. Compromised-agent detection reached 72.27%. ACAGS also supported APPROVE, REVIEW, and REJECT authorization outcomes, with SHAP explanations providing model interpretability. The results demonstrate the potential of combining behavioral intelligence and delegated authorization controls to strengthen simulated agentic-commerce payment security, while highlighting the need for validation using real-world transactions.
why: Synthetic-data agent payment fraud framework; weak evidence.

title: Corpus Quality Improves, Retrieval Utility Does Not: An Ablation of Preprocessing and Refinement in a Speech-to-QA Pipeline
abstract: Practitioners building training corpora with a pipeline of language models keep a preprocessing or refinement (post-process) stage when switching it on raises the corpus quality. We ablate a production pipeline that turns conference speech into question-answer pairs. The preprocessing stage rewrites the transcript, and the refinement stage filters the generated pairs. Switching each on and off gives four corpora from the same 40 Korean medical and finance sessions. On the corpus itself, quality rises as the stages switch on. Four LLM judges and six human domain experts rank the four corpora the same way, and the fully refined corpus leads by +0.18 and +0.22 on a 1-5 scale. We then ask whether that gain carries downstream. We supply each corpus to six models at inference and measure retrieval accuracy. The ranking does not hold. Enabling the transcript rewrite lowers retrieval accuracy by 0.061, the only stage effect that survives correction for multiple comparisons. That stage also reads the whole session, so it almost doubles the cost of one. With both stages on, accuracy does not change. An equivalence test we declared in advance confirms this. The corpus itself is clearly valuable. It lifts retrieval accuracy from 0.231 to 0.748 in every model and domain we test. More than a third of its pairs carry knowledge that neither of two frontier models produces on its own. On our data, the null does not come from weak corpora. A rising score on a rubric of this kind did not predict what the corpus holds for a model.
why: Korean speech-to-QA ablation; finance only tangential.

title: The Hidden Spillovers of AI Infrastructure: Data Centers and Local Healthcare Markets
abstract: The rapid expansion of data centers supporting artificial intelligence (AI) has sparked growing debate over their impacts on local communities. Concerns about pollution and health risks suggest that nearby hospitals may face greater demand. At the same time, data center development brings substantial investment that may improve local socioeconomic conditions and the availability of healthcare. We examine how large data center openings affect nearby hospitals and local healthcare markets, combining U.S. data on hospital operations and nonhospital providers over 2013-2024 in a staggered difference-indifferences (DiD) design. We find that emergency department (ED) visits at nearby hospitals decline by 6.7% following large data center openings, with effects diminishing over distance. In contrast, inpatient utilization and service performance remain relatively stable. Decomposing such decline suggests approximately 85% of the effect can be attributed to reduced county-level ED visits per resident rather than population changes or patient redistribution across those hospitals. We further document growth in physician offices and residential-care facilities, suggesting that greater nonhospital care availability may contribute to the decline in ED demand. The volume reduction is accompanied by financial consequences as nearby hospitals experience a 5.1% reduction in net patient revenue without corresponding reductions in staffing or inpatient workload. Together, our study broadens the debate on data center by providing new evidence on how such development reshapes local healthcare markets, with spillover effects on nearby hospitals. Our findings offer policymakers a more comprehensive perspective for evaluating data center projects and inform hospital managers on demand forecasting and operational planning.
why: Data center effects on hospitals; not finance, no transferable method.

title: Fintech in Banking, Health and Education: Its Impact and the Role of AI Introduction, Review of Literature, Research Gaps and Hypotheses (Draft)
abstract: nd Today, most of us use our mobile phones for various financial activities. We scan the QR code to pay chai-wala, use Google Pay or Phone Pe to transfer money to our friends, pay our college fees online, and renew our insurance policy through an app. These are some of the financial technology or fintech services that have become a part of our lives. A couple of years ago, we had to stand in a queue at the bank counter to make these payments. In India, the journey of digital payments commenced with the introduction of UPI in 2016 and has since gained tremendous popularity among Indians. Fintech started its journey with banking and payment services, but it has since entered other verticals of our lives. Health and education are some of the most important expenses for an average Indian family. A hospital bill can come unexpectedly and be really expensive, and college or coaching fees need to be paid regularly. Hence, today people also use digital payments for hospital bills, online insurance, education loans, and instalment plans for education and health payments. Additionally, in recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has found its way into fintech, helping in detecting fraud, responding to customer inquiries, and determining customer eligibility for loans.
why: Draft fintech overview with literature review; no contribution.

title: Delegated Demand: When the Buyer Is a Verifier. A Demand-Side Theory of Agentic Markets Across Shopping, Hiring, Lending, and Procurement
abstract: When a person hands a choice to an agent, the agent reads the seller's offer as claims it can or cannot check. This paper states delegated demand as the demand side of the Theory of Delegated Markets and reads it across shopping, hiring, lending and capital allocation, and procurement, with healthcare triage as a limiting case. Delegated demand is choice by a decision bearer that applies a rule to inputs on behalf of a distinct welfare bearer, where the weight the rule gives a claim can rise with the bearer's capacity to check that claim against a record outside the offer. That capacity is a variable. At its low end sit the deployed shopping agents that audits show to be moved by description; at its high end sits the procurement rule that must be able to verify what a tenderer states. Five propositions, DD1 to DD5, follow: the division of the offer into a persuasion layer and a proof layer as checking capacity rises, signal degradation ordered by the cost of altering a signal, two-sided delegation with two rule-setters, recursion speed set by the volume of outcomes that re-enter the rule, and verification as the signal toward which a delegated market 2 moves where checking costs less than the claim is worth. Each carries a boundary and a falsifier. Six institutional parameters say how the instances differ, and a field study in a strategy course is specified as a design. To my knowledge, no prior statement treats the verifying agent as the buyer across these four markets; each component has close precursors, which Sections 1 and 5 name.
why: Demand-side theory of agentic markets; no data or implementation path.

title: AI-Driven Multi-Channel E-Commerce Operations and Supply Chain Optimization in the Digital Economy: An Empirical Framework for Emerging Markets
abstract: The rapid expansion of the digital economy has fundamentally transformed traditional retail structures into interconnected, data-driven e-commerce ecosystems. In emerging Southeast Asian markets, enterprises increasingly operate across fragmented digital storefronts, including marketplace platforms (e.g., Shopee, Lazada, Tiki) and social commerce channels (e.g., TikTok Shop). However, managing multi-channel e-commerce operations presents critical challenges in inventory synchronization, dynamic pricing, warehouse fulfillment, and customer retention. This paper proposes an integrated conceptual framework that examines how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and big data analytics optimize e-commerce platform operations within the broader macroeconomic context of the digital economy. By synthesizing theoretical perspectives from Transaction Cost Economics (TCE) and the Resource-Based View (RBV), the study analyzes four core operational dimensions: (1) algorithmic pricing and promotional elasticity across platforms, (2) AI-assisted warehouse and last-mile logistics optimization, (3) automated customer journey personalization, and (4) digital payment risk management. The findings suggest that integrating predictive AI tools into e-commerce back-end operations reduces order fulfillment latency and mitigates multichannel inventory distortion (the bullwhip effect). This study provides actionable strategic insights for e-commerce operations managers, digital economists, and policymakers aiming to foster sustainable digital trade infrastructure.
why: Conceptual e-commerce framework; no empirical finance contribution.

title: Automation, Career Ladders, and Capital Accumulation
abstract: This paper studies automation in a two-period overlapping-generations model with a cognitive and a manual sector, in which only workers who enter a career-track cognitive job when young can hold veteran cognitive jobs when old. Because hiring an entrant also creates a senior position, competition for entrants builds the value of that position into the entry wage, which lies below the manual wage. Since a large entering cohort becomes the stock of incumbents that blocks the next one, youth employment and capital converge through damped oscillations. An advance in artificial intelligence erodes labor's comparative advantage, lowers the marginal product of cognitive labor, and, under a condition that holds in our calibration, extends automation and lowers the return to capital. Employment protection extends automation while lowering the entry wage when part of severance is dissipated in administrative and procedural costs, and lowers capital even when severance is a pure transfer to the worker, because it shifts pay toward old age. In a calibration to the United States, an advance in artificial intelligence that raises the extent of automation by 4.6 percentage points lowers young cognitive employment by more than a third on impact.
why: Overlapping-generations automation theory; no data or finance tooling.

title: HealthGuard-MARL: Emergent Sleeper-Cell Fraud in a Multi-Agent Healthcare Insurance Market A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Real-Time Healthcare Fraud Detection
abstract: Healthcare fraud costs the United States an estimated $300 billion annually [1]. Current detection systems are retrospective and static, failing against adaptive, patient adversaries. We present HealthGuard-MARL, a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework in which a saboteur hospital agent discovers a sleeper-cell fraud strategy: behave honestly to accumulate trust, strike with inflated claims at peak trust, absorb the penalty, and repeat, entirely through reward maximisation, with no scripted fraud instructions. We replicate the Kerr & Cohen (2006, 2009) Value Imbalance attack in a healthcare trust-audit simulation and make four original contributions: (1) a 30-seed significance test demonstrating the strategy is statistically robust (paired t(29) = 9.36, p
why: Multi-agent healthcare fraud simulation; no financial market data.

title: Predicting or Shaping Tastes? Artificial Intelligence, Preference Manipulation, and Welfare in Personalized Markets
abstract: Digital platforms use artificial intelligence both to predict what consumers genuinely prefer and to influence what they perceive as attractive. We develop a monopoly model that separates these channels. Prediction-enabled matching reduces true horizontal mismatch, whereas manipulation reduces perceived mismatch without improving the underlying match and may impose a direct psychological cost. Correctly accounting for the unit mass of consumers generates two pricing regimes. With partial market coverage, the monopoly price is independent of both technologies and prediction and manipulation are privately complementary because both expand perceived demand. Once personalization is strong enough to cover the market, the optimal price rises with personalization and the two technologies become private substitutes. Welfare comparisons are correspondingly regime-dependent. In both smooth pricing regimes, manipulation is privately overvalued relative to its marginal constrained-social contribution, but under partial coverage it can have a positive second-best effect by mitigating monopoly underconsumption. Under partial coverage, prediction is socially undervalued when manipulation is absent or modest, but this wedge can reverse as manipulation becomes stronger; under full coverage, prediction can instead be privately overvalued. A first-best planner that can also control participation never uses manipulation. The policy implication is therefore not a blanket subsidy for prediction combined with a quadratic tax on manipulation: the efficient marginal instruments depend on market coverage and on the extent of behavioral distortion.
why: Monopoly theory of AI preference manipulation; no data.

title: The Cascade Estate: How to finance a service that outlives its chips
abstract: The financing problem in AI infrastructure is not simply that chips become obsolete. It is that the site, equipment, customer promise and investor claim change on different timetables, often without an agreed source of money for the transition. This paper proposes the Cascade Estate: a permanent owner of powered facilities and selected computing equipment that sells a continuing, measurable service rather than the lasting value of a particular chip. Its central mechanism links two cycles. An operating cascade retains, reassigns or replaces equipment according to the complete cost of an accepted result. A financing cycle collects the service revenue, meets finite claims and funds required renewal before distributing the remaining cash. A proposed renewal covenant joins customer affordability, technical qualification and committed funding at the point of each new obligation, with independent verification and controls on order release. Power procurement, capacity rights and counterparty exposures are assessed within that same decision. Public transactions, supplier observations and established operating methods anchor the proposal; missing deal terms and future performance remain named, material assumptions. Thought experiments explain why idle capacity is not necessarily saleable, an upgrade is not automatically growth, and securitisation allocates rather than removes risk. The contribution is an integrated, testable architecture for making technological change financeable while preserving growth choices. It does not require speculative technology or claim a universally profitable estate. Author disclosure (21 October 2026). The author holds shares in NVIDIA Corporation, which is discussed in this paper. This paper presents an independent research proposal, not a recommendation to buy or sell any security. AI assistance. AI-assisted tools supported research, drafting, analytical coding and document preparation. The author is responsible for the final content.
why: Financing model conceptual for AI infrastructure; no empirical content.

title: Green Finance and ESG Performance in Industry 5.0: The Role of Digital Technologies, AI-powered Big Data Analytics, Green Innovation, and Green Transformational Leadership
abstract: The global sustainability transition is faced with an increasingly severe credibility challenge, as green finance and environmental, social and governance (ESG) disclosures outpace the firm's ability to provide verified operational evidence that substantiates their sustainability commitments. This challenge has become increasingly significant for the European Union, as its Industry 5.0 agenda increasingly integrates human-centred industrial transformation, green and digital transitions, AI-enabled innovation, and clean industrial competitiveness, whereas the threat of greenwashing intensifies the need for credible environmental claims. The study utilized a quantitative survey-based approach to analyze 350 managers in Pakistan's internationally connected textile and apparel industry based on PLS-SEM and corroborated all hypotheses established on the natural resource-based view: (1) green finance associate with digital technologies; (2) digital technologies associate with AI-powered big data analytics; (3) AI-powered big data analytics associate with green innovation; (4) green innovation associate with ESG performance; (5) green transformational leadership moderate the association of AI-powered big data analytics and green innovation; and (6) digital technologies, AI-powered big data analytics, and green innovation sequential mediates the relationship of green finance and ESG performance. Our findings encourage firms to deploy green finance not only as a tool for the preservation of the environment but also for the development of blockchain and Internet of Things infrastructure that creates a traceable and transparent supply chain.
why: Survey-based PLS-SEM on Pakistani textiles; no AI-finance method.

title: Artificial Intelligence, State Corporate Governance and the Transformation of Human Autonomy
abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence redistributes power between governments, technology companies and individuals, and whether existing legal frameworks adequately protect autonomy, accountability and equitable access to resources. Through doctrinal and socio-legal analysis, it investigates AI-driven governance using three case studies: the Netherlands’ SyRI welfare-fraud system, European regulatory action concerning Meta’s behavioural advertising, and the United Kingdom’s cloud-infrastructure competition investigation. The paper evaluates the implications of algorithmic decision-making, digital surveillance, corporate influence and AI infrastructure for fundamental rights and distributive justice. It assess institutional control, transparency, accountability and access to remedies. The paper argues that AI’s impact on democracy and social equality depends on how technological power is regulated, distributed and held accountable.
why: Doctrinal legal analysis of AI governance; no finance method.

title: Human-Centric Green Agricultural Technology Adoption in the Industry 5.0 Era: Farmers' Organizations, AI-Sustainability Perceptions and a Finance-Digital Pathway to Green Innovation
abstract: Global agri-food systems are entering the Industry 5.0 era, where artificial intelligence, digital connectivity and advanced analytics increasingly intersect with sustainability, climate resilience and human-centered decision-making. Yet this transition remains uneven across Asia and the Global South, where smallholders and resource-constrained farmers face fragmented access to finance, digital infrastructure, extension services and green technologies. Drawing on the Natural Resource-Based View, this study develops a finance-digital-behavioral mechanism linking Green Finance, Digital Technologies, Farmers' Attitudes toward Sustainable Agricultural Practices and Green Innovation, with AI-Sustainability Perceptions moderating the digital technology-attitude relationship. Using questionnaire data from 350 farmers within the institutional setting of farmers' organizations, with Pakistan serving as the empirical context, and PLS-SEM, the findings show that Green Finance strengthens Digital Technologies (β = 0.461), which enhance sustainable agricultural attitudes (β = 0.319), while these attitudes strongly promote Green Innovation (β = 0.568). The serial indirect effect is significant (β = 0.084), and AI-Sustainability Perceptions strengthen the digital technology-attitude pathway (β = 0.185). The study advances a human-centered Industry 5.0 mechanism in which finance, digital technologies and farmer cognition support inclusive, resilient and environmentally sustainable agricultural transformation, with broader relevance across emerging Asian and Global South agri-food systems.
why: Farmer questionnaire survey on green innovation; off-target.

title: Species-Specific Growing Stock Volume Prediction From Multispectral Airborne Laser Scanning Using A 3D Convolutional Neural Network
abstract: Accurate prediction of species-specific growing stock volumes from airborne laser scanning (ALS) data is essential for operational forest inventory in boreal regions, where pine, spruce and broadleaved species differ substantially in timber quality and ecological function. Multispectral ALS (M-ALS) instruments acquire simultaneous returns at multiple wavelengths, providing both structural and spectral information from a single sensor. So far species-specific volume prediction from M-ALS data has relied on hand-crafted statistical features fed to non-parametric models. This study investigated end-to-end deep learning applied directly to M-ALS voxel representations for species-specific growing stock volume prediction in a boreal forest in Finland. Five configurations of a 3D Inception V3 convolutional neural network were evaluated, ranging from a unispectral single-branch baseline to a multispectral dual-branch architecture combining a 3D voxel branch with a 2D convolutional branch that uses aerial images. All configurations were trained on 595 circular field plots and evaluated on 111 independent test squares. Replacing unispectral ALS input with three simultaneous M-ALS channels produced statistically significant reductions in prediction error across all species volumes. Adding co-registered aerial RGBN (red, green, blue and near-infrared) spectral channels to the multispectral voxel representation produced the largest additional gain for broadleaved species, reducing relative root mean square error from 56.5% to 37.5%. The best configurations matched or exceeded the accuracy of a k-nearest neighbour benchmark with hand-crafted features on identical training and test data, demonstrating that end-to-end deep learning is a viable alternative for species-specific M-ALS forest inventory.
why: Forest volume CNN from laser scanning; unrelated to finance.

title: Toward Agentic AI for the 6G Physical Layer: From Algorithm Discovery to Verified Baseband Silicon
abstract: 6G will be designed faster than it can be built: AI-driven search already proposes physical-layer algorithms at machine speed, while carrying a single one onto embedded baseband silicon remains specialist work. That silicon imposes hard memory and numeric limits, but also exposes cost structures a GPU lacks, and a design flow that never runs on the target sees neither. We present an agentic workflow in which an LLM coding agent implements algorithms on a commercial baseband SoC, optimizes them down to agent-written vector assembly, and validates them on silicon. The agent is guided by a knowledge base of measured platform facts, checked at every step against evaluators it is instructed never to edit, and metered per phase. We showcase the workflow on an AI-discovered orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) detector portfolio on the open 6G4All platform. It yields twelve kernels that run cycle-exactly on silicon, their optimized versions at 18k-405k cycles (30-660 $μ$s) per frame. It also yields a new detector shaped by the chip's measured costs that needs 13.9% fewer cycles than the port of the discovered detector while matching its error rate, with a measured edge our evaluation cannot statistically resolve, a structure that a hardware-blind search objective had no reason to find. What is not specific to OTFS is the workflow: an LLM agent exploring an implementation space under real hardware limits, with the cost of every choice measured rather than assumed.
why: 6G baseband agentic coding; not finance.

title: Credit Where Due Carry Licenses, Full Faith and Credit, and the Post-Bruen Traveler
abstract: In October 2013, a Philadelphia mother with a valid Pennsylvania license drove into New Jersey and spent nearly forty days in jail for it. The Full Faith and Credit Clause did nothing for her, and every court to consider the question since has said it never will. This Article accepts that answer and asks the question it leaves open. A carry license is a grant of permission, and the permission stays home. It is also the record of a State's determination that the holder is qualified, and on the evidentiary reading of the Clause-and under the 1804 statute that still governs executive recordsthat determination is proved in every court in which the holder is prosecuted. The Clause supplies the fact. After New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass'n v. Bruen, the Second Amendment supplies the force. A forum that disregards the determination and makes a licensed traveler in transit submit to a second screening must find a historical tradition behind the demand. The history it will find runs the other way. From Indiana in 1820 to Oakland in 1890, many carry laws-city permit ordinances among them-exempted the traveler on his journey, and the Supreme Court of Texas refused to make him lock his pistol in a trunk. The tradition was narrow: it ended when the journey did. So is the claim this Article makes. Part I maps the Clause's three categories. Part II tests the hardest case, New Jersey's five decades of judge-issued permits, and concedes that it fails as a judgment. Part III builds the theory of evidentiary credit and shows the work it does against the leading justification for duplicative screening. Part IV carries that theory into Bruen and the travelers' tradition and meets the adverse decisions. Part V turns to Congress. The permission does not travel. The determination does, and so does the right. * Jonathan S. Goldstein, Esq. is an attorney with an active, nationwide firearms law practice. He was the co-author of an amicus brief in New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass'n v. Bruen that Justice Alito favorably cited in his concurrence. See 597 U.S. 1, 76 (2022) (Alito, J., concurring). Mr. Goldstein is also a Lecturer in Law at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, from which he graduated and where he teaches a course in firearms law. Mr. Goldstein is also a member of the board of the National Rifle Association. He writes here in his personal capacity and not on behalf of any institution or organization. As many scholars once relied on graduate students to assist with the production of significant scholarship, I rely on an AI assistant. The ideas, research, theme, and supervision of the writing are mine. Some of the drafting may be done with the assistant's help. I also use AI for some of the more mundane organizational tasks behind the production of my written work. My name is on the product and I stand behind the work.
why: Legal analysis of carry licenses; off-topic.
